header.competitor: Unnamed competitor (never named in the interview)
header.incumbent: Existing payments provider (unnamed); support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: Halima, the COO and decider, chose the vendor that brought named people and on-call coverage for on-sales, and dismissed our tiered support plans as "a queue with a faster timer"; our technical proof won the CTO but not her.

evidence.excerpt: Their provider's support was a ticket form. They got a reply after the on-sale was over.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Ben, their CTO, said twice.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: But this was the first time the CEO saw it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: So Monday morning the COO, Halima, says they're replacing payments before the spring on-sales.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: Payments had already failed during on-sales twice and nobody switched, so failure alone was not the trigger. What changed was that the CEO saw it publicly and the incumbent's ticket-form support answered only after the on-sale was over. From day one this was a response-under-pressure problem owned by the COO. It was never mainly a throughput problem owned by the CTO, and we evaluated it as the second.
trigger.messaging: When a prospect switches after an incident, open with what happens in the first minutes of a failure and who responds, not with platform performance.

evidence.excerpt: Halima. Ben wanted us. He told me that, and he told me he lost.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: it was Halima's call and she made it in one meeting.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: So Monday morning the COO, Halima, says they're replacing payments before the spring on-sales.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Ben presented them to her.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Halima set the mandate the Monday after the incident and made the final call. Signals of who would decide were there from the start. We sold to Ben: our strongest proof, the load test, reached Halima only secondhand through him. How much direct time we had with her is unclear beyond the support-plan exchange.
decider.messaging: When an operations executive sets the mandate after an incident, build a decider-level story about incident response and accountability alongside the technical case for the CTO.

evidence.excerpt: A named solutions engineer and an account lead, in the room.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And they said there'd be a shared channel and someone on call for every major on-sale.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before that meeting it was throughput, queueing, bots. After, it was names.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: But I don't know that.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: The competitor did not win on features. They changed the buying criteria in one meeting by bringing the actual account team and promising on-call coverage for every major on-sale. After that meeting the customer's questions moved from technology to names. The rep's theory that they over-promised is unverified by his own admission. Even if it is true, it did not matter, because Halima was buying named people and a stated commitment, and we offered neither.
competitor.messaging: In competitive deals with peak-event businesses, put named account people in front of the decider early and state concretely what coverage they get on their critical days.

evidence.excerpt: Ben's team ran a load test in the sandbox and it went great.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: and I walked her through the support plans. The tiers, the response times.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: so it's a queue with a faster timer.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: good.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: The developer story (M2), the uptime history, and the bot and fraud tooling landed with Ben's team. With the decider they barely registered: her entire reaction to the load test was one word. Our support message (M5: tiers, response times, coverage levels) was the one part Halima engaged with, and she rejected it. She asked for a person, and we answered with a service level.
message.messaging: Rewrite M5 for the buyer who asks "who's my person": lead with a named owner and an escalation path, and treat tiers and response times as backup detail.

evidence.excerpt: so it's a queue with a faster timer.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Right before it we were the favourite.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: I thought the load test had won it.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Before that meeting it was throughput, queueing, bots. After, it was names.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The rep places the loss at Halima's sentence, but his own account shows the criteria had already moved after the competitor's meeting. The sense that we were the favourite came from Ben, who was not deciding. We read champion enthusiasm as a deal signal while the decider was asking a question we had no answer for.
decided.messaging: Treat a shift in the customer's questions toward names, escalation or coverage as a signal that the deal is at risk, and answer it with people and a plan, not more technical proof.

evidence.excerpt: She wanted to see, on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We don't have that as a thing.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I could have built something with our solutions engineer, and I didn't.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I had logos. I didn't have a person.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The deciding gap was not a product capability. It was a missing artifact: a written plan for an on-sale morning covering who is watching, whom she calls, and what happens at minute four. Per the rep, it was buildable and he did not build it. The second gap was proof: M8-style logos versus a reference person who could describe being picked up during a real incident. Whether we can actually offer event-level on-call coverage is not established.
gaps.messaging: Create a peak-event readiness plan asset (named roles, monitoring, escalation, minute-by-minute response) plus a reference customer who can speak to an incident, and offer both whenever a prospect's revenue concentrates in spikes.

evidence.excerpt: A name, not a queue.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Someone who picks up.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Nobody said "support." They said "who."
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The customer's vocabulary was people and moments: who, a name, someone who picks up, on-sale morning. Ours was categories: support plans, tiers, uptime. Halima's line directly devalues the uptime and reliability proof we led with. Our word "support" never appeared in her mouth.
language.messaging: Use the customer's frame of what happens when it's down, and who picks up on your biggest day, in place of "support plans with tiered response times" for operations buyers.

gaps.question: Who was the competitor?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan, or Ben if he is willing, which vendor won, so the loss can be tracked against them.

gaps.question: Did the competitor really commit to on-call coverage for every major on-sale, and was it in writing or the contract?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ben whether the on-call and shared-channel promise appeared in the proposal or contract, or was only said in the meeting.

gaps.question: What did Halima herself weigh in her one-meeting decision?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ben (or Halima, if a loss interview is possible) what she said in the decision meeting and what would have changed her mind.

gaps.question: Could we have offered named people and on-sale on-call coverage if asked?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the solutions engineering and support leads whether a named contact and event-day coverage can be offered, and on what terms.

gaps.question: Did Halima ever meet anyone from our side other than Jordan before deciding?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan who from our team Halima met directly, and whether a solutions engineer was ever in the room with her.

close.rep_takeaway: Your champion's excitement is not the decider's criteria. Once the questions turned to "who," the load test stopped mattering. When a decider asks for a person and a plan, answer with a name and a written plan, and if you know you can build the asset with your SE, build it before the decision meeting, not after.
